newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordanian police break up protest over press law.
newsitem.headline: Jordanian police break up protest over press law.

text.p: Police in riot gear broke up a demonstration against Jordan's new press restrictions on Tuesday, beating and kicking journalists and confiscating cameras.
Witnesses said 10 journalists from foreign and Jordanian news organisations were arrested as they covered the protest near the offices of Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali.
The journalists, including Reuters Television cameraman Khaled Ramahi, were released without charge after eight hours in detention.
A female journalist, beaten as she tried to stop police taking a television camera, was treated for cuts and bruises.

Around 50 demonstrators, waving banners proclaiming "No to the Assassination of Press" and "We will let not let our mouths be gagged and our pens broken", earlier marched on Majali's office but were kept back by police, some in riot gear.

Scuffles broke out when police tried to confiscate television cameras. They beat a woman reporter, kicked and hit others with batons, and wrestled engineers' union chief Laith Shubailat to the ground.

Shubailat, a frequent thorn in the side of Jordanian authorities, is one of 13 influential union bosses who have threatened to resign unless the government revokes recent amendments to Jordan's press law.

The amended press law sets sweeping restrictions on reporting, stiffens fines for offenders and imposes financial obligations on newspapers which journalists say will force most of Jordan's small but vocal opposition weekly papers to close.
Minister of State for Information Samir Mutawae said the police had dispersed the demonstrators because they did not get official permission for the protest.
"The security forces were prepared to let things go, but people were trying to approach the prime minister's office. They were obstructing the road," he told Reuters.

Mutawae was quoted by the official Petra news agency as saying the government, which issued the press law without recourse to parliament, had "no plan whatsoever, in any circumstances, to withdraw any part of the revised press law."
Opposition members of parliament accuse the government of exploiting a parliamentary recess to issue laws on press freedoms and upcoming elections without consultation.

"These are martial laws. The regime is scared," Shubailat told reporters shortly before the violence broke out. "We must get our democratic rights, and we won't get them without struggling, being persecuted and going to prison."

Shubailat was sentenced to death -- and then reprieved -- for attempting to overthrow the government in 1992. He was later sentenced to three years in jail for branding King Hussein a traitor for his peace with Israel, but was released early.
